method: Concert pitch is the written pitch shifted by the instrument's transposition: a Bb trumpet sounds a major 2nd below written, an Eb alto saxophone a major 6th below, an F horn a perfect 5th below, an Eb clarinet a minor 3rd above, and the piccolo, guitar, double bass and contrabassoon move whole octaves. Each instrument is stored as a semitone and letter-step offset so the result keeps a musical spelling: a written Db on a Bb clarinet sounds Cb, while a written C# sounds B. The interval name follows from the letter distance and semitone count, so compound shifts are named as major 9ths and major 13ths, and the concert frequency is 440 x 2^((MIDI - 69) / 12) in 12-tone equal temperament. Notes use scientific pitch notation (C4 is middle C), octaves are limited to -1 to 9 and pitches to MIDI 0-127, and the chart lists every chromatic step of the entered octave. Key signatures, clefs, written accidentals carried through a key change, horn basso and other historical notations, bass-clef readings for bass clarinet, euphonium and tuba, and instrument ranges or playability are not modelled; the calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: S. Adler, The Study of Orchestration, 4th ed. (transposing instruments and written versus concert pitch)
K. Kennan and D. Grantham, The Technique of Orchestration, 6th ed. (transposing instrument families and octave shifts)
A. J. M. Houtsma, Pitch and frequency, in Handbook of Acoustics (equal-tempered frequency relation at A4 = 440 Hz)
